rows.title: Older workers aren’t retiring. Should they be forced to?
rows.standfirst: When workers past retirement age can’t afford to retire — that’s one thing. When they can, and just don’t want to — that’s trickier.

rows.title: Trump renews push to fire Fed Governor Lisa Cook
rows.standfirst: Trump is once again threatening to fire Cook over unproven allegations of mortgage fraud after an earlier effort to remove Cook was struck down by the Supreme Court.

rows.title: I'm just here for the health benefits
rows.standfirst: Dependable health insurance is keeping more people in their jobs. Rising health costs don't help. Today we look at the repercussions this kind of job lock has on the wider economy.

rows.title: Employers unexpectedly cut 23,000 jobs in a sign of a wilting labor market
rows.standfirst: U.S. employers cut 23,000 jobs in July, and job gains for the two previous months were weaker than initially reported, according to a report Friday from the Labor Department.

rows.title: Kalshi and Polymarket bets on clinical trials criticized as 'ghastly'
rows.standfirst: Researchers warn betting on clinical trials could incentivize insider trading and interfere with drug development. But Kalshi and Polymarket say they provide valuable information to patients.

rows.title: Amid cost of living stress, many parents are supporting children well into adulthood
rows.standfirst: Polls show most Americans think young adults today have it harder financially than past generations. A majority of parents help their grown children with expenses, even if it hurts their own finances.

rows.title: Following the Chipotle playbook for the cyclospora crisis
rows.standfirst: Taco Bell and Taylor Farms are taking hits to their reputation due to the cyclosporiasis outbreak across the country. They could learn a thing or two from Chipotle, which went through its own public relations battle during a similar outbreak about a decade ago.

rows.title: World Tour 5: Sand heists and property rights in the Caribbean
rows.standfirst: Imagine a nation where, for the residents, land is for the claiming. You walk down the street, pick out a nice looking plot of land, and just plop down a marker. No rent, no taxes, no deed – just free land. That’s the communal system of property rights that governed a small Caribbean island for over a century.

rows.title: Sand heists and property rights in the Caribbean (Summer School)
rows.standfirst: Imagine a nation where, for the residents, land is for the claiming. You walk down the street, pick out a nice looking plot of land, and just plop down a marker. No rent, no taxes, no deed – just free land. That’s the communal system of property rights that governed a small Caribbean island for over a century.

rows.title: How ending TPS is squeezing workers, businesses and (soon) consumers
rows.standfirst: What happens when roughly a million people working legally in the U.S. suddenly lose that right to stay here? We’re starting to find out in places like Miami, Florida, home to one of the largest Haitian communities in the country. There, we talk to people on what the end of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) means for their businesses and the wider economy.

rows.title: SpaceX's revenue rises as its once-soaring stock price drifts back to Earth
rows.standfirst: On their first earnings call since SpaceX's June public offering, executives said the company is pouring funds into rocket development, Starlink satellites and AI.

rows.title: The sneaky economics of healthwashing
rows.standfirst: Why food companies love labels like "organic" and "high protein," why our brains are misled by them — and how to avoid paying extra for marketing.

rows.title: Why Texas is betting 'Y'all Street' can take on Wall Street
rows.standfirst: Dallas' financial industry is growing amid a larger Texas business boom. But can it really steal New York's crown?

rows.title: Why we're short on blood, water and helium
rows.standfirst: Shortages are in the news again! Here’s why the supply of blood, water and helium are at concerningly low levels.

rows.title: This lawyer believes in second chances. Now AI is providing a boost
rows.standfirst: Tens of millions of Americans have criminal records that can be barriers to employment. An AI-powered app is helping those eligible to expunge their records at a pace not seen before.

rows.title: You bet your life insurance
rows.standfirst: Some of the biggest firms on Wall Street are, at this very moment, waiting for thousands of strangers to die to reap their returns. Because there’s a market for life insurance policies. And it’s legal.

rows.title: We learned 5 important things about the economy this week
rows.standfirst: From inflation, to credit card debt, to who's actually doing the spending: These are key takeaways from this week in economic news.

rows.title: Retiree benefits bump, credit repayment slump, and a dating app in the dumps
rows.standfirst: It’s Indicators of the Week!

rows.title: Feds probe 'mention markets' amid White House Kalshi controversy
rows.standfirst: Betting on what people say is becoming an increasingly popular category of prediction market sites. Now, federal officials have opened a probe examining whether those markets are a magnet for manipulators.

rows.title: C is for C-shaped economy
rows.standfirst: Which letter best describes how the U.S. economy is shaped: C or K? We examine the arguments for both and why there’s so much disagreement over who’s faring best in today’s economy.

rows.title: Trump sued over service selling faster access to Truth Social posts
rows.standfirst: The federal lawsuit alleges that the service from the president's media company violates the Constitution. Meanwhile, Trump Media executives say they have signed up more than 10 customers.

rows.title: Inflation eases in July as gasoline and grocery prices fall
rows.standfirst: Consumer prices in July were up 3.4% from a year ago — a smaller annual increase than in May or June. The news makes it less likely the Fed will feel the need to raise interest rates in September.

rows.title: Here's how gyms, salons and ice cream are changing America's Main Streets
rows.standfirst: Shoppers' changing habits are fueling a major shift in what types of businesses are occupying storefronts.

rows.title: AI chatbots are offering financial advice. Should you trust them?
rows.standfirst: Experts say AI can get personal finance fundamentals right but may struggle with nuanced questions.

rows.title: World Tour 6: Currency Chaos in Argentina
rows.standfirst: Just about everyone in Argentina is an expert in inflation and whether they like it or not, economic flexibility. Can we learn from them?

rows.title: Currency Chaos in Argentina (Summer School)
rows.standfirst: Just about everyone in Argentina is an expert in inflation and whether they like it or not, economic flexibility. Can we learn from them?

rows.title: Consumers are mad as hell and aren't gonna take it anymore
rows.standfirst: Rage. That’s what consumers are feeling right now. A new survey found consumer complaints hit a record high this year. Another from last year found a huge share of consumers felt ‘rage’ with a product or service problem. Just think about the modern consumer experience: hidden fees, ballooning customer support wait times (perpetually experiencing higher call volumes than usual) … shrinkflation! Argh!! What’s going on?

rows.title: The secret economics inside the new Planet Money board game
rows.standfirst: From Nobel Prize-winning research to the Laffer Curve, Scabby the Rat, Veblen's peacock, and more — the economic ideas and inside jokes hiding throughout Planet Money's new board game.

rows.title: Borrowing money to invest! What could go wrong?
rows.standfirst: The total amount of investors using margin aka borrowing money to help pay for a trade is at an all time high of over $1.5 trillion. Is this something we should worry about? We spoke to Jurrien Tinner at Fidelity Investments.

rows.title: Spending money shouldn't make you feel bad. But if it does, read this comic
rows.standfirst: If spending — or not spending — money makes you feel shame or regret, you might be grappling with financial guilt. Financial planner Lauryn Williams breaks down three types and how to deal.

rows.title: What to know about this weekend's IndyCar race on the National Mall
rows.standfirst: Why is the car race in this part of D.C.? Will it be streaming? Who's paying for it? Here's what to know before the Freedom 250 Grand Prix hits the National Mall this weekend.

rows.title: EV sales slow, US Treasury yields grow, 'Niu Lai' has impressive box office mojo
rows.standfirst: This week’s indicators: EV sales sputter in North America but flutter internationally; U.S. Treasury Yields … RISE!; a low-budget movie so terrible, it became a box office hit in China.

rows.title: The U.S. national debt is $40 trillion. Are Americans paying for it?
rows.standfirst: The US national debt has soared to $40 trillion - a record high.

rows.title: 3 things to know about the $40 trillion federal debt
rows.standfirst: The U.S. federal debt hit a record $40 trillion this week. The debt has doubled since 2017, and just paying interest on the accumulated debt now costs the government more than $1 trillion a year.

rows.title: The bond market is signaling trouble ahead. This is why you should pay attention
rows.standfirst: Many people don't pay attention to bond markets, but they should — especially now. This is why they matter and why the drop in bond prices is signaling investor concerns about the U.S. economy.

rows.title: Proposed California wealth tax sparks debate: Will billionaires leave the state?
rows.standfirst: A proposed first-of-its kind tax would target California's nearly 250 billionaires in an effort to fund health care. If voters pass it, will the state's economy suffer?

rows.title: Chinese court sentences founder of property developer Evergrande to life in prison
rows.standfirst: Chinese property developer Hui Ka Yan has been sentenced to life in prison. The decision marks a milestone in Evergrande's saga after it collapsed with more than $300 billion in liabilities.

rows.title: Is bankruptcy really all that bad?
rows.standfirst: Bankruptcy has a negative stigma surrounding it. But what if we told you it’s not as bad as you may think? In fact, economists think we should actually see more of it!

rows.title: Whistleblower Arturo Béjar leads testimony in landmark trial against Meta
rows.standfirst: The former Meta employee testified that the company culture prioritized user numbers over child safety measures.

rows.title: Data shows women are leaving the workforce. What does that say about the economy?
rows.standfirst: For decades, one of the most reliable trends in the American economy has been the growing number of women working.

rows.title: The U.S. debt tops a record-shattering $40 trillion. Yes, with a T
rows.standfirst: The federal debt reached $40 trillion as the government adds red ink at a rapid rate. That's leading nervous investors to demand higher interest rates — pushing up borrowing costs for everyone else.

rows.title: FCC's lone Democrat says Disney 'has found its courage' in lawsuit against agency
rows.standfirst: The Walt Disney Company is suing the FCC, alleging a violation of First Amendment rights by challenges to its ABC broadcast licenses. NPR's Leila Fadel speaks with FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez.

rows.title: World Tour 7: Getting entrepreneurial in Korea
rows.standfirst: This week’s stop on our world tour - Korea. A country divided into two very different power structures since the end of WWII. Today South Korea is the maker of some of the world’s favorite exports – from Samsung TV’s to BTS. But 75 years ago it was a much different story. How the textile industry and a partnership with Bangladesh lifted the country out of poverty and paved the way for rapid economic growth.

rows.title: Getting entrepreneurial in Korea (Summer School)
rows.standfirst: This week’s stop on our world tour - Korea. A country divided into two very different power structures since the end of WWII. Today South Korea is the maker of some of the world’s favorite exports – from Samsung TV’s to BTS. But 75 years ago it was a much different story. How the textile industry and a partnership with Bangladesh lifted the country out of poverty and paved the way for rapid economic growth.

rows.title: Have a bad manager? Science explains why.
rows.standfirst: The best manager isn’t necessarily the best employee. Turns out it isn't so easy to predict what DOES make a good manager. Today on the show, we turn to science to help answer that very question.

rows.title: Kalshi bans former congressman George Santos for life after State of the Union trades
rows.standfirst: Kalshi says Santos did not cooperate with its investigation into bets he placed on his own attendance at the State of the Union. The company also fined the disgraced congressman more than $71,000.

rows.title: The U.S. sues Amazon again
rows.standfirst: Federal regulators and 22 states allege that the tech giant made billions by manipulating how much brands and sellers paid for ads on its platform.

rows.title: How ICE arrests are creating 'economies of fear'
rows.standfirst: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested nearly 50,000 people in July, marking the biggest month for ICE arrests of President Trump’s second term. We talk to a researcher who thinks this increased ICE activity is creating an “economy of fear” in cities around the country — and has the data to prove it.

rows.title: How a comic book store got swept into the tariff storm
rows.standfirst: Tariffs continue to rile all kinds of American businesses more than a year after Trump unveiled his first set of tariffs — including a comic book store owner in Ohio.

rows.title: Dolly Parton’s “9 to 5,” the true story behind the anthem (bonus)
rows.standfirst: The brilliance of "9 to 5" is that it is catchy even though it’s also kinda depressing. You will be dancing along. You're enjoying it. And, then when you really listen to the lyrics, you're like, Wait, this is messed up. This is real. This is a problem we need to fix. Like, why does it have to be this way?

rows.title: Branded fruit: How produce got “Honeycrisp-ified"
rows.standfirst: The produce aisle is changing. You’ve noticed this, I’m sure. It is now full of superstar fruits and vegetables: The Honeycrisp apple, The Cotton Candy grape, The Cuties mandarin orange. They stand out. They cost more. They have branding and sometimes trademarks and patent-ish kinds of protections.

rows.title: Fed's Kevin Warsh warns inflation is too high, sparking bets rate hikes are coming
rows.standfirst: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh reiterated his commitment to fighting inflation in a major speech — raising expectations that rate hikes may be coming, though he did not clearly spell out a path going forward.

rows.title: U.S. says pipelines will make Strait of Hormuz irrelevant. Energy experts disagree
rows.standfirst: Treasure Secretary Scott Bessent said oil pipelines will make Strait of Hormuz irrelevant in two years. Energy experts say that is unlikely to happen.

rows.title: Businesses are getting tariff refunds. Why aren't consumers getting their cut?
rows.standfirst: A slew of American companies are getting billions of dollars back in tariff refunds after a Supreme Court ruling. Many consumers, though, may never get anything back.

rows.title: The teacher pay penalty, Meta's major settlement, and a footwear flop
rows.standfirst: This week’s indicators: The teacher pay penalty; Meta’s massive settlement; Nike and Dick’s Sporting Goods are struggling.

rows.title: The stakes are high as Kevin Warsh is set to give his first major speech as Fed Chair
rows.standfirst: The stakes are high as Fed Chair Kevin Warsh prepares to give a speech on Friday at the annual gathering of economists and central bankers in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

rows.title: School districts face a back-to-school math problem: The high price of diesel
rows.standfirst: With the war in Iran driving up fuel prices, diesel is now nearly $5.60 a gallon, affecting school districts at the start of the year.

rows.title: Coyote vs. Acme finally gets its big break
rows.standfirst: Coyote vs. Acme will finally get its theatrical release on Friday after a years-long saga involving supposed tax write-downs, negotiations and multibillion-dollar studio deals. It's a drama almost straight out of a Hollywood screenplay. Today we have the story from the inside. This episode is an update of an episode from December 2023.

rows.title: Can a landmark settlement protect children from social media?
rows.standfirst: The owner of Facebook and Instagram has agreed to change the way its platforms work. Can those changes be enforced? And are they enough to protect the mental health of young people?

rows.title: The White House's preferred economic tools are hitting snags
rows.standfirst: Tariffs and export controls have been the Trump administration's main economic security tools. Neither is working very well right now.
